newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-GERMAN FEDERATION PAID GRAF APPEARANCE FEES.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-GERMAN FEDERATION PAID GRAF APPEARANCE FEES.

text.p: The German Tennis Federation (DTB) conceded on Tuesday it had paid world number one Steffi Graf hundreds of thousands of dollars in appearance money -- a practice banned by the women's tour.
DTB general secretary Guenter Sanders was giving evidence to the court trying Graf's father on charges of tax evasion.

He told the court, trying to establish how much money was funnelled abroad out of the reach of tax authorities, that Peter Graf had been paid between $150,000 and $270,000 a year for "services and advertising" in connection with DTB-run events in Hamburg and Berlin between 1990 and 1993.
Asked if this was mostly money paid to ensure the tournaments had a big-name attraction, Sanders replied "Yes".
The news weekly Der Spiegel said at the weekend the widespread payment of appearance money to all top women players was an open secret.

It said Steffi Graf and joint number one Monica Seles each commanded between $30,000 and $400,000 to play in an event, depending on its size, with players ranked down to number 13 receiving correspondingly less.
The anecdotal examples cited by Der Spiegel from records produced in connection with Peter Graf's trial added up to a total of well over $2 million in appearance payments.
While many smaller events need to pull in big stars to sell tickets, the Women's Tennis Association (WTA) has banned the payment of appearance money for fear it damages the players' competitiveness.

WTA Tour rules state that "No player, agent, coach or family member shall accept money or anything of value that is given from any sources, directly or indirectly, to influence or guarantee her appearance..."

The rules stipulate a fine of at least $50,000 and a ban of up to 90 days for each offence, together with repayment of the money. Organisers who pay appearance money can lose the right to stage the tournament.

Peter Graf is accused together with family tax adviser Joachim Eckardt of evading 19 million marks in taxes by failing to declare some 42 million marks of his daughter's earnings between 1989 and 1993. He could face a jail sentence of up to 10 years.
His daughter is also under investigation, although she says she left her financial affairs to her father from an early age.

The Connecticut-based WTA, in a statement from chief executive Anne Person Worcester on Tuesday, insisted it was "inappropriate" for them to comment on specific issues while the Graf trial was in progress.
"To date the Tour is not aware of any substantiated evidence of appearance money being paid to any Tour player," she said.
"The Tour is monitoring the ongoing trial, and if any evidence warrants further investigation, the Tour would conduct an investigation."
